claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The untreated alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility and exhibits brittle failure.
Dislocations pile up at sharp internal phase boundaries in the untreated alloy.
Dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries cause localized stress concentrations, microcracking, and brittle failure during room-temperature tension.
Annealing at approximately 700 °C for 30 minutes under argon, followed by rapid quenching, is an appropriate intervention.
The annealing treatment produces moderate interfacial elemental redistribution and diffusion at lamellar colony boundaries.
Interfacial diffusion smooths compositional gradients and reduces sharp compositional and structural mismatch at the boundaries.
Smoothing the interfaces reduces the barrier to dislocation motion.
Annealing alleviates the mismatch in mechanical properties between the constituent phases.
The modified interfaces promote continuous dislocation transmission instead of dislocation pile-up.
Reduced dislocation pile-up lowers local stress concentrations and delays microcrack initiation.
Delayed microcrack initiation prevents catastrophic damage during straining.
The treatment will significantly improve room-temperature tensile ductility, potentially doubling a ductility metric relative to the untreated material.
The treatment will maintain or modestly enhance yield strength relative to the as-cast alloy.
The proposed benefits apply under quasi-static room-temperature tensile testing.
Excessive diffusion could coarsen the lamellae or form deleterious phases.
An inappropriate annealing window could degrade the lamellar microstructure or reduce strength.
The quantitative ductility and strength changes depend on the precise alloy composition and annealing parameters.
